segments.title: The Fog and the Court: Opening into Chancery's Grip

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a series dedicated to one of the strangest, most magnificent novels in the English language.
Over the coming episodes, we're going to live inside Dickens's world — its fog, its courts, its secrets, and its extraordinary people.
Today we begin at the beginning — with the fog rolling in over London and the Court of Chancery tightening its grip.
I'm joined by three people who know this novel deeply and love it fiercely, each from a different angle.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive — he hears this prose the way a musician hears a score.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as an anatomy of power — every institution a machine for keeping the poor where they are.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read this novel five times and still finds sentences that stop her cold.
Let's begin where Dickens begins — in the fog, in the court, in the muck.
The moment you open Bleak House — really open it, read it aloud — you realise Dickens is doing something almost reckless.
He gives you ten pages of fog before he gives you a single human being.
And yet it works — because the fog IS the argument.
There's a character I find endlessly fascinating as a performer — and that's Tulkinghorn.
Dickens describes him slipping between the great country house and his London chambers with a kind of supernatural indifference.
Listen to how he puts it — this is the prose doing something extraordinary.
"He walks into Chesney Wold as if it were next door to his chambers and returns to his chambers as if he had never been out of Lincoln's Inn Fields."
He melts in; he melts out — Dickens actually uses that word, melts, twice in the same paragraph.
The man is practically a fog himself.
Oliver is right that Tulkinghorn is fog — but I'd want to be precise about what kind of fog.
He is the fog that the powerful use to move between their worlds without being seen.
Chesney Wold and Lincoln's Inn Fields — aristocratic land and the law — are not separate kingdoms for Tulkinghorn.
They are two rooms in the same house — and he owns the key to both.
And the Court of Chancery operates on the same principle — it appears to be a system of justice, but it is a system of delay.
Consider the flatness of this exchange — Dickens strips it to bare procedure.
"The Jarndyce in question," said the Lord Chancellor, still turning over leaves, "is Jarndyce of Bleak House."
Still turning over leaves — he doesn't even look up.
The fate of an entire family — their inheritance, their identity, their lives — delivered as a footnote.
That is what the institution looks like from inside its own logic — and Dickens knew exactly what he was showing us.
What strikes me — rereading this opening — is how early the novel starts playing its games with names.
Bleak House itself — the name — is doing so much work before we've even arrived there.
And there's this wonderful, unsettling little scene with Krook — the rag-and-bottle man — in which Esther watches him write letters in the air.
He writes out the word Jarndyce, she reads it — then he rubs it out and writes Bleak House.
And Dickens tells us, simply —
"These, in some astonishment, I also read; and he laughed again."
He laughed again — it's the again that gets me every time.
This old man already knows something Esther doesn't — the novel is riddled with that asymmetry, right from the start.
And there's something in that laugh — something gothic, something gleeful — that never quite leaves you.
Caroline, you're absolutely right — and as a performer, Krook is one of the great gifts Dickens leaves lying about.
He's a grotesque, yes — but he's also a mirror of the Lord Chancellor himself.
Dickens even says so outright — calls Krook the Lord Chancellor of his own court, surrounded by his own suitors.
The difference is — one is played for horror and the other for farce.
And Dickens can never quite decide which is which — which I think is entirely the point.
I want to push on that — because I think what Dickens is doing with these parallel figures is more pointed than mere satire.
Krook hoards paper, can't read it, holds it until it rots.
Chancery hoards documents, processes them endlessly, produces nothing of use to the people who need them.
That's not satire — that's a structural diagnosis.
Dickens understood — even if he'd have resisted the language — that the law doesn't malfunction.
It functions exactly as it was designed to — for the benefit of those who can wait, and the ruin of those who cannot.
That's a distinction worth sitting with — the difference between a system that fails and a system that succeeds at the wrong thing.
We'll carry that through everything we discuss today — and in the next segment we'll move deeper into the novel's two narrators and the extraordinary formal experiment Dickens is running.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Machinery of Injustice: How Chancery Crushes Richard

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great sprawling masterpiece apart — slowly, carefully, with genuine pleasure.
Today's segment is called The Machinery of Injustice — and we're asking a very particular question: how does Chancery actually destroy a person?
Not abstractly. Not statistically. But one specific young man — Richard Carstone — watched in real time.
With me today, as always, are three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has arguably read more Dickens aloud than any living person.
Oliver brings the performer's ear — the rhythms, the comic timing, the moments the prose demands to be heard rather than read.
Dr. Daniel Rosen — cultural historian and perhaps the most rigorous anatomist of class and power in this novel.
Daniel reads every institution in Bleak House as a mechanism — and he's never wrong about that.
And Caroline Woodcourt — critic, five-time reader of this novel, and the person in the room most likely to make you stop and actually feel what Dickens is doing.
Let's begin with the engine room. Daniel — Chancery as a system. What is it actually doing to Richard?
What Chancery does to Richard is not an accident — it is precisely what the system is designed to do.
It converts a living person into a function of the suit. It takes his energy, his hope, his capacity for relationship — and redirects all of it toward itself.
And the passage that captures this with terrifying precision is Richard's speech to Vholes in chapter thirty-nine.
He says: "he becomes to me the embodiment of the suit; that in place of its being an abstraction, it is John Jarndyce."
That is a diagnosis of what ideology does to a mind under extreme pressure.
Richard cannot locate the actual enemy — the Court, the lawyers, the centuries of accumulated legal mystification — so he displaces it onto a person he trusted.
The system has made John Jarndyce the face of its own cruelty. And Richard believes it.
And what's so devastating about that speech, from a performer's point of view, is the voice Dickens gives it.
It begins with such earnest retrospective warmth — "If any man had told me when I first went to John Jarndyce's house" — and you can hear the young Richard in that, the hopeful boy he was.
Then it turns — "So little did I know of the world!" — and that exclamation mark is doing extraordinary work.
It's self-pity, yes, but it's also a man genuinely bewildered by his own transformation.
When I've read this aloud, there's a point where the voice has to break slightly — not melodramatically — just a hairline fracture in the rhythm.
Because Dickens has written a man who doesn't know he's dying. And that is the saddest thing he does in this book.
What strikes me every time I re-read that passage is who Richard is saying it to.
He's confiding in Vholes. Of all people. The man who is professionally invested in keeping this delusion alive.
Richard has lost his capacity to distinguish between a friend and a predator. That's the measure of the damage.
And Dickens makes Vholes so brilliantly, insidiously quiet throughout all of this.
He doesn't argue with Richard. He doesn't encourage or discourage. He simply receives this speech — like a machine receiving fuel.
Caroline, that is exactly right — and it connects to a structural point about how the whole class system operates in this novel.
Look at how Dickens describes Sir Leicester Dedlock — an ostensibly benevolent master, generous in his own estimation.
And yet the novel tells us plainly — he supposes all his dependents to be, and here I'll read it exactly —
"utterly bereft of individual characters, intentions, or opinions, and is persuaded that he was born to supersede the necessity of their having any."
That is not a portrait of a cruel man. It is a portrait of a system that has convinced a decent man that erasing other people is simply the natural order.
Richard and Sir Leicester are not equivalent figures — but they are both caught inside structures larger than their own intentions.
That word "supersede" is doing something very specific in that sentence, isn't it.
It's a bureaucratic, legal word. It belongs to documents and courts and instruments of power. Not to human beings.
And Dickens keeps doing that — he keeps giving the language of the law to the people who are supposed to be above it.
Which brings me to Tulkinghorn — possibly my favourite villain in all of English literature, and I don't say that lightly.
Dickens introduces him in chapter twenty-seven with this extraordinary compressed portrait. Let me read it as it deserves —
"Rustily drest, with his spectacles in his hand, and their very case worn threadbare. In manner, close and dry. In voice, husky and low. In face, watchful behind a blind."
Four fragments. No verbs of action. Just — here he is. Immovable. Ancient. And the irony Dickens drops at the end is devastating:
"The peerage may have warmer worshippers and faithfuller believers than Mr. Tulkinghorn, after all, if everything were known."
"If everything were known." That's the whole novel in four words.
What I find so unsettling about Tulkinghorn is the portrait he turns to in chapter thirty-nine — Lady Dedlock's likeness on the wall.
He examines it. And then he says, so casually, as if commenting on the weather —
"'Lady Dedlock.' Ha! A very good likeness in its way, but it wants force of character."
"It wants force of character." He is looking at a painting and he is really looking at her secrets. At her vulnerability.
And then he says "Good day" and leaves. That exit is almost unbearably sinister.
Because he has just told Lady Dedlock — without telling her anything — that he knows exactly who she is.
And notice that Tulkinghorn's power is entirely illegitimate — in the sense that it operates outside any formal office.
He holds no title. He represents no client's actual interests in that moment. He is simply a repository of secrets that he has never been asked to hold.
This is how informal power actually operates. Not through laws but through information asymmetry — knowing what others don't know you know.
And Dickens understood, writing in the 1850s, that this was how aristocratic England actually functioned. Not through noble pronouncements. Through files.
And then — as if to cleanse the palate entirely — Dickens gives us Skimpole.
Harold Skimpole, who is the most cheerful parasite in English fiction and who has elevated self-exemption from moral life into a kind of performance art.
There's a passage where Esther captures his philosophy — and it is so perfectly, so gleefully awful — let me read it:

"what Harold Skimpole was, Harold Skimpole had found himself, to his considerable surprise, when he first made his own acquaintance; he had accepted himself with all his failings and had thought it sound philosophy to make the best of the bargain."
"To his considerable surprise!" That is masterful comic writing. The surprise is fake, of course — Skimpole has never examined himself for a moment.
But the fake surprise is the whole performance — the constant enactment of a man too delightful and spontaneous to be held responsible.
He is the comic obverse of Richard — where Richard is consumed by a system he cannot escape, Skimpole escapes every system by simply refusing to acknowledge it exists.
And Dickens gives us another version of that evasion — though far less funny — in old Mr. Turveydrop.
Where Skimpole plays at being a child, Turveydrop plays at being a grand benefactor — always dispensing largesse that isn't his to dispense.
There's a scene where he addresses Caddy — his exhausted daughter-in-law who is actually keeping him in comfort — with this magnificent fraudulent generosity.
"Do not even allow my simple requirements to be considered if they should at any time interfere with your own, my Caroline. Your necessities are greater than mine."
"Your necessities are greater than mine" — spoken by a man whose every necessity Caddy is in fact meeting.
It's the language of self-sacrifice used to enact self-service. And Dickens delivers it "in a burst of deportment" — that detail is perfect.
The theatrical gesture is the exploitation. They are the same thing.
What Caroline is describing is a recurring structure in this novel — the performance of duty as a cover for its exact opposite.
Turveydrop invokes "Deportment" — that absurd Regency relic — as a kind of authority that exempts him from material obligation.
Sir Leicester invokes hereditary dignity. Chancery invokes the authority of centuries of law. Skimpole invokes his own irresponsibility.
Different idioms. One function. To extract from those beneath them without accountability.
So what we have in this segment — and this is something Dickens is doing quite consciously, I think — is a whole taxonomy of evasion.
The system doesn't need a single villain. It has Tulkinghorn's cold files, Leicester's serene blindness, Skimpole's performed innocence, and Turveydrop's counterfeit generosity.
And at the centre of it all — Richard Carstone, who trusted the system and is being consumed by it, one delay at a time.
Coming up: we'll look at the women in this novel who see all of this clearly — and what it costs them to see it.

segments.title: A Passion for the Law: Richard's Ambition and Its Cost

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart — slowly, carefully, and with enormous pleasure.

I'm your host, and today we're looking at one of the novel's most quietly devastating arcs: the story of Richard Carstone, a young man of genuine gifts, consumed by an institution designed to consume him.
Joining me are three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more Dickens audiobooks than any living person, and he comes to Richard with a performer's ear — he hears what the prose is doing before he explains it.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as a precise anatomy of class power — he'll show us exactly how the machinery around Richard works, and who benefits.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel — she's the one who will make sure we feel what Esther feels, watching someone she loves disappear.
Let's begin with the question of Richard's character — what he has, and what he lacks, and whether the distinction even matters.
The thing that makes Richard's story so painful to read is that Dickens never lets you doubt that he's genuinely likeable.
Esther is not a narrator who flatters people — she's too honest for that — so when she says she liked him more and more the better she knew him, you believe her completely.
But Dickens plants the diagnosis very early, and it's a structural one — it's not Richard's fault in any simple sense.
Listen to what Esther actually says about his education.
"The system which had addressed him in exactly the same manner as it had addressed hundreds of other boys, all varying in character and capacity."
That phrase — the system — is doing so much work.
Richard isn't destroyed by his own nature; he's destroyed by a system that refused to see him as an individual.
And Chancery, of course, will do exactly the same thing — just more thoroughly.
Caroline has put her finger on something essential, and I want to follow that thread about the system, because Dickens is making a very specific argument here.
The educational system and the legal system are not analogies for each other — they are the same system, reproduced at different scales.
Both exist to process human beings in bulk, to produce uniform outputs regardless of individual difference, and to punish any quality that can't be standardised.
Dickens gives us the most beautiful sentence for what this does to Richard.
"They were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were very bad masters."
That's not a moralistic diagnosis — that's a structural one.
Richard's qualities were never trained to serve him — and so they serve whatever system gets to him first.
Chancery gets to him first.
There's a moment earlier in the novel that I always think about alongside these passages — one that's rather more delicious, because it comes from the least reliable narrator imaginable.
Harold Skimpole, who hasn't an honest bone in his body, nevertheless gives you what might be the most accurate psychological portrait of Richard in the entire novel.
He describes Richard's relationship to Common Sense — personified, as only Skimpole could — as a man with a ruled account-book in his hand, resembling a tax-gatherer.
And then — here's where Dickens is being brilliantly wicked — Skimpole has Richard say this.
"I see a golden prospect before me; it's very bright, it's very beautiful, it's very joyous; here I go, bounding over the landscape to come at it!"
You laugh — you have to laugh — and then you feel slightly sick about having laughed.
Because that is Richard, precisely — bright, beautiful, bounding — and we already know what's waiting for him.
It's the cruelest thing about Skimpole: he's never quite wrong.
That's beautifully put — and what unsettles me about that Skimpole passage is that Dickens makes it almost impossible to hold the right amount of irony in your head.
Skimpole is monstrous — we know that — but he's also funny, and Richard's portrait of himself as someone bounding over landscapes is genuinely touching as well as doomed.
What Dickens does in the later chapters is strip the comedy away very gradually.
By the time we get to Esther's account of Woodcourt visiting Richard at Symond's Inn, the light has almost entirely gone.
Esther says something that I find almost unbearable to read.
"It revived a fear I had had before that my dear girl's little property would be absorbed by Mr. Vholes and that Richard's justification to himself would be sincerely this."
Sincerely this — meaning that Richard genuinely believes he is protecting Ada, even as he destroys everything that is hers.
He's not lying to her. He's lying to himself.
And that is precisely where Vholes enters — not as a villain in any melodramatic sense, but as a system made flesh.
What Dickens does with the Vholes passages is formally extraordinary — he doesn't just characterise the man, he performs the institutional logic that protects him.
Listen to Kenge's speech — which is really the speech of the entire legal establishment — when reform is suggested.
"Now you cannot afford — I will say, the social system cannot afford — to lose an order of men like Mr. Vholes."
The slide from 'you' to 'the social system' — that's the whole move.
Your interests and the system's interests are declared identical — and the man who is eating Richard alive becomes a pillar of social order.
And then Dickens adds that devastating parliamentary inquiry, ending with the one answer that — quote — 'proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years.'
'Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a most respectable man.'
Respectability is not a moral quality in this novel. It is a weapon.
The parliamentary inquiry passage is one of the great comic set-pieces in English prose — and I say that as someone who has read it aloud more times than I can count.
The question numbers alone — 'Question number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight hundred and sixty-nine' — that is pure music.
Dickens is doing something brilliant: using the deadpan language of bureaucracy to expose how perfectly bureaucracy insulates itself from consequence.
The witness is 'not prepared to say' that the procedures cause vexation — because they have never given him any.
He is entirely honest — and his honesty is the most damning thing in the passage.
The system works perfectly for the people inside it.
Richard is not inside it. He is the raw material.
Raw material — that phrase stays with you.

What you've all traced is a kind of double devastation: Richard's gifts turned against him by education, and then that very susceptibility exploited by an institution which has made exploitation its entire operating principle.
In our next segment, we'll look at what it means to watch all of this — to be Ada, or Esther — and whether the novel offers any form of witness that isn't itself a kind of helplessness.

segments.title: Illegitimacy and Secrets: The Architecture of Lady Dedlock's Fear

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great labyrinthine novel apart — one chamber at a time.
Today we're descending into the architecture of concealment — illegitimacy, secrets, and the peculiar terror that structures Lady Dedlock's entire existence.
With me, as ever, are three remarkable readers of this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps any living person, and he brings a performer's ear for what the prose is actually doing at the level of sound and rhythm.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads Bleak House as a systematic anatomy of class power — and Lady Dedlock, he'll tell us, is not exempt from that anatomy.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic who has lived with this novel since her teens — she knows its emotional geography intimately, and she reads aloud with extraordinary care.

Caroline, I want to begin with you — because the Lincolnshire passage is one of the great atmospheric openings in all of Dickens, and it introduces Lady Dedlock through landscape before we even know what she's hiding.
What strikes me every time I return to that passage is that Dickens doesn't describe the landscape — he drowns us in it.
Every sentence is another layer of wet and cold and muffled silence.
And then he gives you this extraordinary line about Lady Dedlock's own windows — let me read it exactly as he wrote it.
"The view from my Lady Dedlock's own windows is alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink."
Lead-coloured and Indian ink — those are the colours of writing, of documents, of legal paper.
And her view — her whole outer world — is made of them.
What she is hiding is itself a kind of legal document — a fact of birth, of record — and the landscape keeps spelling it out.
That's exactly right, and what a performer notices first is the percussion in that passage.
Dickens is writing for the ear — always, always for the ear — and listen to what he does with the rain on the Ghost's Walk.
"The heavy drops fall — drip, drip, drip — upon the broad flagged pavement, called from old time the Ghost's Walk, all night."
Three drops — three stresses — and then that extraordinary name arrives: the Ghost's Walk.
It's a metronome, but the thing it's counting down to is a reckoning.
And then — the masterstroke — she sees the keeper's lodge.
A woman chasing a child through rain to meet a man coming through a gate.
The most ordinary domestic scene imaginable — and it puts her quite out of temper.
I want to hold on to that image for a moment — because what undoes Lady Dedlock is not an abstraction.
It's a working-class family doing what working-class families do: living, moving, keeping warm.
She is childless — Dickens tells us so in parentheses, almost as if it were a legal notation — and everything she surveys is predicated on that fact.
The Dedlock estate, the title, the entire social edifice, rests on her performance of a woman without a past.
But the class system that imprisons her is the same system that she and Sir Leicester embody and enforce.
She is simultaneously its most refined product and its most endangered secret.
And that tension — between the performance and the secret — is exactly what makes the scene where she comes to Esther through the wood so unbearably charged.
Esther is sitting at her favourite spot, watching the Ghost's Walk in the distance, and then she notices a figure approaching through the trees.
Dickens slows the recognition down — almost cruelly — through Esther's narration.
"By little and little it revealed itself to be a woman's — a lady's — Lady Dedlock's."
Three steps of recognition, each one tightening the screw.
A woman — a lady — Lady Dedlock: it's a whole social hierarchy collapsed into a single sentence.
And the detail that she is walking faster than usual — that tiny deviation from composure — tells us everything about the cost of what she's about to do.
The tricolon — woman, lady, Lady Dedlock — is pure theatrical technique, and I suspect Dickens knew exactly what he was doing with it.
He gave his public readings enormous thought about where to slow and where to accelerate — and that sentence is a controlled deceleration to a name.
But the passage I keep returning to when I think about Lady Dedlock's inner life is the Tulkinghorn scene — the one where he simply watches her and thinks.
She has drunk water with a steady hand — nothing to express weakness — and reclined in her chair with her face shaded.
"This woman," thinks Mr. Tulkinghorn, standing on the hearth, again a dark object closing up her view, "is a study."
He is closing up her view — literally blocking her light — and calling it scholarship.
That's Dickens's portrait of surveillance: cold, self-congratulatory, and utterly without mercy.
Tulkinghorn is the novel's most precise image of how the law functions as an instrument of domination — not through violence, but through knowledge.
He doesn't need to act yet.
The mere fact that he knows — that he can act, at any moment of his choosing — is sufficient to break her.
And notice what she does: she pours water with a steady hand.
She eats nothing, but the hand is steady.
The body is in open rebellion — no appetite — but the performance of composure continues with iron discipline.
She has been performing that composure her entire adult life, and it is the only weapon she has left.
What I find almost unbearable is how that performance poisons everything it touches — including Esther's own story.
Esther inherits her mother's illegitimacy as a social fact — and that fact shadows every relationship she has, including her prospect of marriage to Allan Woodcourt.
Mrs. Woodcourt — Allan's mother — is obsessed with pedigree, with Welsh lineage, with the idea that her son's blood must not be compromised.
And Jarndyce's challenge to her — the speech he gives Caroline about what legitimacy actually means — is one of the most quietly radical moments in the entire novel.

"Come you, and see my child from hour to hour; set what you see against her pedigree, which is this, and this — and tell me what is the true legitimacy when you shall have quite made up your mind on that subject."
The true legitimacy — he wrests the word entirely away from birth and plants it in character, in daily life, in what you see from hour to hour.
It's a direct refutation of everything the Dedlock world stands for.
That speech is one of the moments where I think Dickens genuinely outruns his own instincts as a social conservative.
He believes in institutions, in property, in the natural order — and yet here he produces a direct attack on the doctrine of blood as a measure of worth.
The secret Lady Dedlock has spent her life concealing is, in the end, not a sin — it's an accident of the system that the system then uses to destroy her.
She is punished not for what she did but for what she was: a woman who loved outside the law before the law had finished defining her.
And Dickens makes sure we feel the full weight of that punishment.
The Ghost's Walk that drips all night in that first Lincolnshire passage — it ends at a gate, in the cold and the mud, with Lady Dedlock dead.
And that, I think, is what separates Dickens from every other Victorian novelist writing about fallen women.
He doesn't sermonise.
He makes you grieve.
That movement — from the dripping terrace at Chesney Wold to the cold gate where she dies — is one of the great architectural arcs in all of Victorian fiction.
We'll be returning to how Dickens structures foreshadowing and fate in a later segment.
But next, we turn to the other great web of concealment in Bleak House — the Chancery suit itself, and what it does to the people caught inside it.

segments.title: Mud, Disease, and Silent Witness: Jo's Testimony to Society's Neglect

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart sentence by sentence — and puts it back together with fresh eyes.
I'm your host, and today we're turning to one of the novel's most quietly devastating threads: the figure of Jo, the crossing-sweeper — anonymous, illiterate, expendable.
Jo is Dickens's most sustained argument against a society that produces suffering and then looks away.
With me today are three readers who've thought deeply about this novel and about what it means that a boy like Jo exists at all.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive — he hears the prose the way a musician hears a score, and no one reads Dickens aloud with more conviction.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as an anatomy of class power — every institution in the novel, he argues, is a mechanism for keeping the poor in their place.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens — she brings to it the close reader's gift: the ability to stop at a sentence and say, listen to that.
Let's begin where the novel places Jo at his most tender and most terrible — in the final weeks of his life, nursed by the most unlikely of caregivers.
Oliver, this passage in Chapter Forty-Seven is extraordinary — can you walk us into it?
What Dickens does in this passage — and he does it with such apparent ease that you almost miss the craft — is assemble the most improbable gallery of witnesses around a dying child.
You have Phil Squod, this sooty, one-eyebrowed armourer, simultaneously hammering at his little table and checking on a boy he barely knows.
Dickens gives him one line, delivered with a nod of the green-baize cap, and it's the whole scene in miniature.
Listen to what it actually says:
"Hold up, my boy! Hold up!"
Three words, said twice, from a man who looks like he's been fired out of a cannon — and somehow it's one of the most moving things in the book.
That's Dickens the performer. He knows exactly what the voice can carry that the page alone cannot.
What strikes me is the social geometry of that room, and what it reveals about who actually cares for the destitute in this novel.
Phil Squod, George the trooper, Woodcourt — these are all figures who exist at the margins of respectability or just below it.
The people with real institutional power — the lawyers, the philanthropists like Mrs. Jellyby — are conspicuously absent from this room.
Dickens can't say this directly, so he says it through the architecture of compassion: who shows up and who doesn't.
And then comes the line that floors me every time I read this passage.
"How strangely fate has entangled this rough outcast in the web of very different lives."
That word — outcast — is doing enormous work. Dickens isn't calling Jo unfortunate. He's naming what the system has made him.
And the web — that's not a neutral metaphor. It's the same structural trap as Chancery, as the law, as everything that binds this novel together.
I want to come back to that word 'web,' because Daniel is absolutely right — but I think there's also something almost tender in it.
Jo is entangled, yes. But he's also, for perhaps the first time in his life, held by something.
What I find unbearable — and I mean that in the best sense, the sense of a novel doing its job — is the detail of the trooper in the doorway.
Dickens writes that from his "superfluity of life and strength" George seems to shed down temporary vigour upon Jo.
"From his superfluity of life and strength, seeming to shed down temporary vigour upon Jo."
That word 'temporary' — it's a blade hidden in a kind sentence.
We know, and Dickens knows we know, that no amount of vigour lent from George can make this anything other than a stay of execution.
Caroline, yes — and what I'd add, as someone who's read this passage aloud more times than I can count, is that the rhythm of it is itself a kind of breath-giving.
Dickens keeps the sentences moving — Phil doing this, George filling the doorway — there's almost no pause, no rest, and then suddenly: Jo speaks more robustly.
That small rally in Jo's voice is the entire passage's emotional punchline. And Dickens delivers it without ceremony, just slips it in.
He trusted his readers to feel the weight of a boy speaking 'more robustly' when we know he is dying. That trust is what makes him great.

I want to pull the lens back for a moment, because Jo doesn't exist in isolation — he's produced by a system, and Dickens keeps showing us that system at work even in its most apparently benign expressions.
Take the Dedlock world — which is as far from Jo's crossing as you can get, and yet Dickens insists on the connection.
There's a small, devastating passage in Chapter Twelve where Mrs. Rouncewell — the housekeeper, a woman of genuine dignity — is quietly measured against Lady Dedlock's coldness.
Dickens couches it in the politest possible language:
"Mrs. Rouncewell is not quite sure as to that... Mrs. Rouncewell thinks she would be more affable."
That hesitation — 'not quite sure as to that' — is the English class system in miniature.
Mrs. Rouncewell cannot say outright that Lady Dedlock is cold, because the hierarchy forbids it. So she wraps the truth in deference and hopes the reader catches it.
And the reader does catch it — because Dickens has made very sure they will.
What I love about that passage is the way Dickens nests the criticism inside the praise. Rosa gushes — 'so affable, so graceful, so beautiful, so elegant' — and the repetition itself becomes suspect.
By the time Mrs. Rouncewell delivers her quiet reservation, we've already been primed to distrust the superlatives.
And what connects this, for me, to Jo — is the question of who is permitted to tell the truth in this novel, and how.
Jo can't read, can't write, can't testify in his own person. Mrs. Rouncewell can speak, but only through layers of hedging.
Dickens is the only one in the novel who can say it straight — and he does, but always through the characters, never for himself.
That's beautifully put, Caroline — and it's why, when Jo finally does speak at length near his death, the moment carries such accumulated weight.
Dickens has spent hundreds of pages establishing that Jo has no voice, no standing, no place.
And so when George enters that doorway and Jo speaks 'more robustly' — that tiny act of speech is everything.
I've performed this novel for hundreds of audiences. And every single time, that word — 'robustly' — makes people hold their breath.
Because they know what's coming. Dickens has made them know.
What emerges from all of this — the deathbed vigil, the muted housekeeper, the web of entangled lives — is a portrait of a society that has no language adequate to what it has done to Jo.
Dickens invents one anyway: he builds it out of green-baize caps, temporary vigour, and the quiet flinch of a loyal housekeeper.
Oliver, Daniel, Caroline — thank you. Next, we'll turn to the question of Esther herself, and the remarkable narrative act of giving this novel two competing centres of consciousness.

segments.title: Names, Secrets, and the Law's Web: How Dickens Knots It All Together

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's great fog-bound novel and try to see clearly through it.
Today we're asking how Dickens binds everything together — the secrets, the names, the legal machinery, the gossip — into one extraordinary knot.
With me are three remarkable readers of this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive, and he hears the prose the way a musician hears a score.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in Bleak House as a machine for protecting the powerful at the expense of the poor.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and returns to it the way one returns to a complicated friend.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because when we talk about how Dickens knots things together, the rag and bottle shop and its aftermath seems like the right place to start.
The rag and bottle shop passage is one of the great comic set-pieces in English fiction, and I don't think it gets nearly enough credit.
Dickens turns an entire neighbourhood into a single collective organism driven by nothing but curiosity and greed.
And the joy of it is the specificity — the imagined guineas pouring out of tea-pots, the bank notes stuffed into old mattresses.
He gives us the sentence that sets it all perfectly, and I think it deserves to be read aloud.
"Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus' purse of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop."
Fortunatus' purse — a magical purse that is never empty.
Dickens is telling you that gossip is the currency of the poor — and in this court, it flows and flows and never runs out.
And notice: all that ferment, all that energy, and the court discovers nothing.
Oliver's right to emphasise the comedy, but I'd push a little further into what the comedy is actually doing.
The court imagines treasure because it lives in genuine want.
The fantasy of guineas in tea-pots isn't absurd — it's the only form of wealth redistribution these people can conceive of.
And meanwhile the Smallweeds are actually there, every day, nine hours a day, methodically extracting value from Krook's estate.
The poor court watches and invents fairy tales.
The Smallweeds work.
That division of watchers and extractors — that is the novel's anatomy of class right there.
What I keep coming back to in that passage is the sheer infectious pleasure of it.
Little Swills doing patter allusions to hidden treasure at the Harmonic nights.
Miss Melvilleson pointing her head towards next door while singing about dogs loving broo — whatever broo is.
It's a whole neighbourhood transforming a legal mystery into entertainment, into art, into community.
And Daniel is right that the comedy has a bitter undertow.
But I also think Dickens genuinely loves them for it — for taking something grim and making it sing.
That's exactly right, and it points to something deeper in how the novel handles secrets.
Because the rag and bottle shop is essentially a comic version of the novel's central metaphysics.
There are documents somewhere that will transform everything — everyone can feel it — but no one can get at them.
Which is Chancery.
And it's Tulkinghorn.
Here is how Dickens describes him — and I promise you, this is one of the most perfectly turned character descriptions in all of Victorian fiction.
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every limb.
Not his mind, not his profession — his body.
He doesn't carry secrets — he is made of them.
The passage goes even further than that, and the next sentence is the one that interests me most.
Dickens asks the question directly: is Tulkinghorn devoted to his great clients, or does he sell them nothing but professional services?
And the answer is — we are told — his personal secret.
"He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself."
He is his own client.
That is the legal system in miniature.
The law presents itself as a neutral instrument — it serves the powerful, the Dedlocks, the great families.
But it is in fact serving itself, accumulating knowledge, hoarding it, weaponising it.
Tulkinghorn is not a servant of the aristocracy — he is its parasite and its jailer simultaneously.
That phrase — his own client — stops me every time.
Because it's also a description of Lady Dedlock, isn't it?
She, too, believes herself to be impenetrable — her own inscrutable self, managed by no one.
And yet Dickens shows us, with devastating comic precision, exactly how wrong she is.
There's that extraordinary passage early in the novel — she supposes herself to be, in Dickens's phrase, an inscrutable Being.
"Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices, follies, haughtinesses, and caprices."
The list is so merciless.
Weaknesses, prejudices, follies, haughtinesses, and caprices — five nouns, each one a small knife.
The sentence that follows that passage is the one I love to read aloud above almost any other in Dickens.
The jewellers, the mercers, the librarian — they all speak in reported speech, with that wonderful repetition.
"You must come to us, because we know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it fashionable."
The rhythm of that — the smugness, the absolute confidence — you can hear the shopkeeper's bow in every syllable.
And then Dickens adds, of Mr. Sladdery, that he does not exaggerate at all — which is the deadliest joke in the passage.
Because Sladdery is perfectly right.
He can turn them round his finger.
The great lady, for all her hauteur, is a product being managed by her vendors.
And this is where Dickens earns the description of radical, I think, even if he wouldn't have used the word himself.
The aristocracy in Bleak House is not sovereign.
It is managed — by the law, by trade, by fashion, by anyone who studies it closely enough.
The Dedlocks think they are the summit of the world.
Dickens shows us that they are in fact a market — and Tulkinghorn is both their custodian and their most dangerous creditor.
Knowledge — of Lady Dedlock's secret above all — is the currency that matters.
And when the debt comes due, it destroys her.
I want to bring in Skimpole here, because he complicates the picture in a way I find almost unbearably interesting.
He is the character in the novel who most consciously exempts himself from all of this — from debt, from duty, from the whole system of accountabilities.
And Esther, who is one of the novel's great moral intelligences, finds him enchanting.
She can't quite work out why he isn't subject to ordinary moral obligations, and Dickens gives us the confusion beautifully.
"I was confused by not exactly understanding why he was free of them."
That is such honest narration.
She doesn't pretend to see through him immediately.
She just admits: he was very clear about being free of them — and somehow that was enough.
Skimpole's great trick is that he speaks of himself in the third person — as if Skimpole were a character in a story, not a man with obligations.
It's the same thing Tulkinghorn does, in a sense — they both perform non-accountability.
Tulkinghorn through impenetrability, Skimpole through whimsy.
Both are absolutely free of the moral web — and both leave disaster in their wake.
Dickens understood something profound: the most dangerous people are those who have persuaded themselves — and others — that the rules don't apply to them.
There's a class dimension to this as well, though.
Skimpole's exemption from duty depends entirely on the generosity — the exploitation, really — of those around him.
Someone always pays for Skimpole's freedom.
And we find out, eventually, that he sold Jo to Bucket for five pounds.
The child who has nothing, who exists at the very bottom of this society — Skimpole trades him away to preserve his own frictionless life.
That is the system in miniature again — charm as extraction.
Charm as extraction — that is a phrase I want to return to.
What we're mapping here is a kind of ecology of secrets — every character either hoards them, sells them, or is destroyed by them.
And Dickens has arranged this vast novel so that the threads all pull on each other — gossip in the court, power in Tulkinghorn, self-exemption in Skimpole — and eventually everything tightens.
We'll pick up that tightening — and what it costs — in our next segment.

segments.title: Redemption in Ruin: What Bleak House Leaves Us With

utterances.text: We've spent this episode inside the machinery of Bleak House — the fog, the law, the lives ground down by Chancery's indifference.
Now, as we reach the closing chapters, I want to ask what the novel actually leaves us with.
Is there redemption in Bleak House? Or something darker — a ruin that simply endures?
Daniel, you've been sitting with some of the novel's most devastating images of what Chancery actually produces in the world.
I think you should start us off.
Thank you. What I keep returning to is a passage most readers skim past — Jarndyce describing a street of property nominally belonging to the suit.
It sounds like a legal technicality. It is anything but.
Dickens gives us the sentence that I think is the true verdict on Chancery — not the court scenes, not the lawyers' speeches.

"It is a street of perishing blind houses, with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their hinges and falling asunder, the iron rails peeling away in flakes of rust, the chimneys sinking in, the stone steps to every door — and every door might be death's door — turning stagnant green."
That is what the system makes. Not injustice in the abstract — actual houses, actual decay, actual green rot on stone.
And then Jarndyce delivers the line that opens it outward: these are the Great Seal's impressions, all over England — the children know them.
The children know them. The dispossessed have always known what the powerful prefer to call a procedural matter.
That phrase — the children know them — does something to me every single time.
Because it's said almost gently, by Jarndyce, who is himself a casualty of the suit. There's no rage in it. Just grief.
And yet Dickens doesn't leave us only in that ruin. There's a passage near the end that I find almost unbearably tender.
Jarndyce — this man who has lost so much to a name, to a legal fiction — turns and asks Esther something very simple.
"When you came in, I was full of it. When shall we give Bleak House its mistress, little woman?"
He's reclaiming the name. Bleak House ceases to be a curse and becomes an invitation.
That's not sentimental resolution. That's a man choosing, deliberately, to act as if repair is possible.
I don't want to be churlish about Jarndyce — he's one of Dickens's genuinely good men.
But I think we have to hold those two passages together. One street of perishing houses, one tender question about a wedding date.
The private gesture of repair exists inside a system that is still producing ruin at scale. Dickens knows this.
The Great Seal is still stamping its impression across England while Jarndyce and Esther light candles in their small warm room.
Daniel is absolutely right, and I want to add a third image — because there's a figure in this novel who I think holds the whole tension together.
Tulkinghorn.
Dickens describes his rooms as a kind of portrait of the man himself. And one detail has haunted me since the first time I read it aloud.
"Everything that can have a lock has got one; no key is visible."
Eight words to describe a man, a profession, an entire class that runs on secrets and withholds them as a form of power.
What Jarndyce is trying to do — with Esther, with Bleak House — is precisely the opposite. He is trying to unlock something.
The novel doesn't tell us he succeeds permanently. But the gesture is real, and Dickens renders it with complete seriousness.
The lock and key image — I've never heard it put quite that way before, and now I can't unhear it.
What strikes me about the novel's ending — not just the Jarndyce resolution, but the whole final movement — is how much Dickens trusts the reader to hold the grief and the warmth simultaneously.
He doesn't resolve the contradiction. He makes the contradiction the point.
The perishing houses are still there. And so is the question: when shall we give Bleak House its mistress?
That feels like exactly the right place to end — not with resolution, but with the novel holding its contradictions open, as Dickens always insists on doing.
Perishing houses and a warm invitation. The Great Seal and a small domestic hope. Both true. Both necessary.
My thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt — three guides I'd trust through any labyrinth, Chancery included.
Bleak House Unpacked will return. Until then, keep reading — and keep noticing what the children already know.

From the verdant undulations and the spreading oaks of the Dedlock
property, Mr. Tulkinghorn transfers himself to the stale heat and
dust of London. His manner of coming and going between the two places
is one of his impenetrabilities. He walks into Chesney Wold as if it
were next door to his chambers and returns to his chambers as if he

c39:p29.text:
“Mr. Vholes! If any man had told me when I first went to John
Jarndyce’s house that he was anything but the disinterested friend he
seemed—that he was what he has gradually turned out to be—I could
have found no words strong enough to repel the slander; I could not

Whereas now I do declare to you that he becomes to me the embodiment

c7:p7.text:
The present representative of the Dedlocks is an excellent master. He
supposes all his dependents to be utterly bereft of individual
characters, intentions, or opinions, and is persuaded that he was
born to supersede the necessity of their having any. If he were to
make a discovery to the contrary, he would be simply stunned—would
never recover himself, most likely, except to gasp and die. But he is
an excellent master still, holding it a part of his state to be so.
He has a great liking for Mrs. Rouncewell; he says she is a most
respectable, creditable woman. He always shakes hands with her when
he comes down to Chesney Wold and when he goes away; and if he were
very ill, or if he were knocked down by accident, or run over, or
placed in any situation expressive of a Dedlock at a disadvantage, he
would say if he could speak, “Leave me, and send Mrs. Rouncewell
here!” feeling his dignity, at such a pass, safer with her than with
anybody else.
c7:p7.summary: Sir Leicester is an excellent but blind master who denies his servants any individuality, yet ironically trusts and respects Mrs. Rouncewell above all others in distress.
c7:p7.best_quote: he supposes all his dependents to be utterly bereft of individual characters, intentions, or opinions

change in him, of course. Rustily drest, with his spectacles in his
hand, and their very case worn threadbare. In manner, close and dry.

Skimpole had found himself, to his considerable surprise, when he

dear Caroline”—he would turn to his daughter-in-law with infinite
generosity and protection—“want for nothing, my love. Frame a wish
and gratify it, my daughter. Everything this house contains,

Richard very often came to see us while we remained in London (though
he soon failed in his letter-writing), and with his quick abilities,
his good spirits, his good temper, his gaiety and freshness, was
always delightful. But though I liked him more and more the better I
knew him, I still felt more and more how much it was to be regretted
that he had been educated in no habits of application and
concentration. The system which had addressed him in exactly the same
manner as it had addressed hundreds of other boys, all varying in
character and capacity, had enabled him to dash through his tasks,
always with fair credit and often with distinction, but in a fitful,
dazzling way that had confirmed his reliance on those very qualities
in himself which it had been most desirable to direct and train. They
were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously
won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were
very bad masters. If they had been under Richard’s direction, they
would have been his friends; but Richard being under their direction,
they became his enemies.
c17:p0.summary: Esther reflects on Richard's natural talents being undermined by his lack of discipline, a problem rooted in an educational system that addresses all students identically rather than according to individual capacity.
c17:p0.best_quote: They were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were very bad masters.

passion of the man, the fresh blood of the man, Rick—and Ada, and
little Cobweb too, for you are all interested in a visitor—that I
speak of,” he pursued. “His language is as sounding as his voice. He
is always in extremes, perpetually in the superlative degree. In his
condemnation he is all ferocity. You might suppose him to be an ogre
from what he says, and I believe he has the reputation of one with
some people. There! I tell you no more of him beforehand. You must
not be surprised to see him take me under his protection, for he has
never forgotten that I was a low boy at school and that our
friendship began in his knocking two of my head tyrant’s teeth out

be here this afternoon, my dear.”

“Do you think so!” returned Mr. Skimpole. “Don’t say that, don’t say
that. Let us suppose him keeping company with Common Sense—an
excellent man—a good deal wrinkled—dreadfully practical—change for
a ten-pound note in every pocket—ruled account-book in his
hand—say, upon the whole, resembling a tax-gatherer. Our dear
Richard, sanguine, ardent, overleaping obstacles, bursting with
poetry like a young bud, says to this highly respectable companion,
‘I see a golden prospect before me; it’s very bright, it’s very
beautiful, it’s very joyous; here I go, bounding over the landscape
to come at it!’ The respectable companion instantly knocks him down
with the ruled account-book; tells him in a literal, prosaic way that
he sees no such thing; shows him it’s nothing but fees, fraud,
horsehair wigs, and black gowns. Now you know that’s a painful
change—sensible in the last degree, I have no doubt, but
disagreeable. I can’t do it. I haven’t got the ruled account-book, I
have none of the tax-gathering elements in my composition, I am not
at all respectable, and I don’t want to be. Odd perhaps, but so it
is!”
c37:p115.summary: Vholes admits Richard's attendance will not help, yet offers no objection.

was so very much impressed by the strength of Richard’s anxiety on
this point that in telling me generally of his first visit to
Symond’s Inn he particularly dwelt upon it. It revived a fear I had
had before that my dear girl’s little property would be absorbed by
Mr. Vholes and that Richard’s justification to himself would be
sincerely this. It was just as I began to take care of Caddy that the

c39:p4.text:
But not perceiving this quite plainly—only seeing it by halves in a
confused way—the laity sometimes suffer in peace and pocket, with a
bad grace, and DO grumble very much. Then this respectability of Mr.
Vholes is brought into powerful play against them. “Repeal this
statute, my good sir?” says Mr. Kenge to a smarting client. “Repeal
it, my dear sir? Never, with my consent. Alter this law, sir, and
what will be the effect of your rash proceeding on a class of
practitioners very worthily represented, allow me to say to you, by
the opposite attorney in the case, Mr. Vholes? Sir, that class of
practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth. Now you
cannot afford—I will say, the social system cannot afford—to lose
an order of men like Mr. Vholes. Diligent, persevering, steady, acute
in business. My dear sir, I understand your present feelings against
the existing state of things, which I grant to be a little hard in
your case; but I can never raise my voice for the demolition of a
class of men like Mr. Vholes.” The respectability of Mr. Vholes has
even been cited with crushing effect before Parliamentary committees,
as in the following blue minutes of a distinguished attorney’s
evidence. “Question (number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight
hundred and sixty-nine): If I understand you, these forms of practice
indisputably occasion delay? Answer: Yes, some delay. Question: And
great expense? Answer: Most assuredly they cannot be gone through for
nothing. Question: And unspeakable vexation? Answer: I am not
prepared to say that. They have never given ME any vexation; quite
the contrary. Question: But you think that their abolition would
damage a class of practitioners? Answer: I have no doubt of it.
Question: Can you instance any type of that class? Answer: Yes. I
would unhesitatingly mention Mr. Vholes. He would be ruined.
Question: Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a respectable
man? Answer:”—which proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years—“Mr.
Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man.”
c39:p4.summary: Mr. Kenge's rhetorical defense of legal practitioners like Vholes is presented, along with a mock parliamentary inquiry that demonstrates how institutional self-interest defeats reform through the invocation of Vholes's respectable reputation.
c39:p4.best_quote: Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth.

c2:p2.text:
My Lady Dedlock has returned to her house in town for a few days
previous to her departure for Paris, where her ladyship intends to
stay some weeks, after which her movements are uncertain. The
fashionable intelligence says so for the comfort of the Parisians,
and it knows all fashionable things. To know things otherwise were to
be unfashionable. My Lady Dedlock has been down at what she calls, in
familiar conversation, her “place” in Lincolnshire. The waters are
out in Lincolnshire. An arch of the bridge in the park has been
sapped and sopped away. The adjacent low-lying ground for half a mile
in breadth is a stagnant river with melancholy trees for islands in
it and a surface punctured all over, all day long, with falling rain.
My Lady Dedlock’s place has been extremely dreary. The weather for
many a day and night has been so wet that the trees seem wet through,
and the soft loppings and prunings of the woodman’s axe can make no
crash or crackle as they fall. The deer, looking soaked, leave
quagmires where they pass. The shot of a rifle loses its sharpness in
the moist air, and its smoke moves in a tardy little cloud towards
the green rise, coppice-topped, that makes a background for the
falling rain. The view from my Lady Dedlock’s own windows is
alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink. The vases
on the stone terrace in the foreground catch the rain all day; and
the heavy drops fall—drip, drip, drip—upon the broad flagged
pavement, called from old time the Ghost’s Walk, all night. On
Sundays the little church in the park is mouldy; the oaken pulpit
breaks out into a cold sweat; and there is a general smell and taste
as of the ancient Dedlocks in their graves. My Lady Dedlock (who is
childless), looking out in the early twilight from her boudoir at a
keeper’s lodge and seeing the light of a fire upon the latticed
panes, and smoke rising from the chimney, and a child, chased by a
woman, running out into the rain to meet the shining figure of a
wrapped-up man coming through the gate, has been put quite out of
temper. My Lady Dedlock says she has been “bored to death.”
c2:p2.summary: Lady Dedlock returns to her Lincolnshire estate before departing for Paris, where the landscape is depicted as relentlessly dreary and sodden; her observation of a family scene at a keeper's lodge disrupts her usual composure.
c2:p2.best_quote: The view from my Lady Dedlock's own windows is alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink

c36:p18.text:
I was resting at my favourite point after a long ramble, and Charley
was gathering violets at a little distance from me. I had been
looking at the Ghost’s Walk lying in a deep shade of masonry afar off
and picturing to myself the female shape that was said to haunt it
when I became aware of a figure approaching through the wood. The
perspective was so long and so darkened by leaves, and the shadows of
the branches on the ground made it so much more intricate to the eye,
that at first I could not discern what figure it was. By little and
little it revealed itself to be a woman’s—a lady’s—Lady Dedlock’s.
She was alone and coming to where I sat with a much quicker step, I
observed to my surprise, than was usual with her.
c36:p18.summary: As Esther rests at her favorite spot, a woman emerges through the wood—Lady Dedlock, approaching with unusual haste and emotion.

c48:p105.text:
For a little while they are silent. Lady Dedlock has eaten no dinner,
but has twice or thrice poured out water with a steady hand and drunk
it. She rises from table, takes a lounging-chair, and reclines in it,
shading her face. There is nothing in her manner to express weakness
or excite compassion. It is thoughtful, gloomy, concentrated. “This
woman,” thinks Mr. Tulkinghorn, standing on the hearth, again a dark
object closing up her view, “is a study.”
c48:p105.summary: In the silence that follows, Lady Dedlock maintains thoughtful composure while remaining emotionally turbulent; Tulkinghorn regards her as a fascinating psychological study.
c48:p105.best_quote: This woman,' thinks Mr. Tulkinghorn, standing on the hearth, again a dark object closing up her view, 'is a study.'

c64:p35.text:
“Hush, little woman! Don’t cry; this is to be a day of joy. I have
looked forward to it,” he said exultingly, “for months on months! A
few words more, Dame Trot, and I have said my say. Determined not to
throw away one atom of my Esther’s worth, I took Mrs. Woodcourt into
a separate confidence. ‘Now, madam,’ said I, ‘I clearly perceive—and
indeed I know, to boot—that your son loves my ward. I am further
very sure that my ward loves your son, but will sacrifice her love to
a sense of duty and affection, and will sacrifice it so completely,
so entirely, so religiously, that you should never suspect it though
you watched her night and day.’ Then I told her all our
story—ours—yours and mine. ‘Now, madam,’ said I, ‘come you, knowing
this, and live with us. Come you, and see my child from hour to hour;
set what you see against her pedigree, which is this, and this’—for
I scorned to mince it—‘and tell me what is the true legitimacy when
you shall have quite made up your mind on that subject.’ Why, honour
to her old Welsh blood, my dear,” cried my guardian with enthusiasm,
“I believe the heart it animates beats no less warmly, no less
admiringly, no less lovingly, towards Dame Durden than my own!”
c64:p35.summary: Jarndyce explains how he told Mrs. Woodcourt of Esther and Woodcourt's love, challenged her prejudices about pedigree, and ultimately convinced her to see Esther's true worth and character.
c64:p35.best_quote: 'Now, madam,' said I, 'come you, knowing this, and live with us. Come you, and see my child from hour to hour; set what you see against her pedigree, which is this, and this'—for I scorned to mince it—'and tell me what is the true legitimacy when you shall have quite made up your mind on that subject.'

c47:p105.text:
Phil Squod, with his smoky gunpowder visage, at once acts as nurse
and works as armourer at his little table in a corner, often looking
round and saying with a nod of his green-baize cap and an encouraging
elevation of his one eyebrow, “Hold up, my boy! Hold up!” There, too,
is Mr. Jarndyce many a time, and Allan Woodcourt almost always, both
thinking, much, how strangely fate has entangled this rough outcast
in the web of very different lives. There, too, the trooper is a
frequent visitor, filling the doorway with his athletic figure and,
from his superfluity of life and strength, seeming to shed down
temporary vigour upon Jo, who never fails to speak more robustly in
answer to his cheerful words.
c47:p105.summary: Phil Squod nurses Jo while working as an armourer; Mr. Jarndyce and Allan visit frequently; General George visits often, and all reflect on how Jo became connected to their lives.
c47:p105.best_quote: how strangely fate has entangled this rough outcast in the web of very different lives

c12:p36.text:
That evening, in the housekeeper’s room, Rosa can do nothing but
murmur Lady Dedlock’s praises. She is so affable, so graceful, so
beautiful, so elegant; has such a sweet voice and such a thrilling
touch that Rosa can feel it yet! Mrs. Rouncewell confirms all this,
not without personal pride, reserving only the one point of
affability. Mrs. Rouncewell is not quite sure as to that. Heaven
forbid that she should say a syllable in dispraise of any member of
that excellent family, above all, of my Lady, whom the whole world
admires; but if my Lady would only be “a little more free,” not quite
so cold and distant, Mrs. Rouncewell thinks she would be more
affable.
c12:p36.summary: That evening, Rosa praises Lady Dedlock effusively; Mrs. Rouncewell confirms most of this but privately feels Lady Dedlock could be warmer and more affable.
c12:p36.best_quote: Mrs. Rouncewell is not quite sure as to that...Mrs. Rouncewell thinks she would be more affable.

c39:p58.text:
Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus’ purse
of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop.
Regularly, every morning at eight, is the elder Mr. Smallweed brought
down to the corner and carried in, accompanied by Mrs. Smallweed,
Judy, and Bart; and regularly, all day, do they all remain there
until nine at night, solaced by gipsy dinners, not abundant in
quantity, from the cook’s shop, rummaging and searching, digging,
delving, and diving among the treasures of the late lamented. What
those treasures are they keep so secret that the court is maddened.
In its delirium it imagines guineas pouring out of tea-pots,
crown-pieces overflowing punch-bowls, old chairs and mattresses
stuffed with Bank of England notes. It possesses itself of the
sixpenny history (with highly coloured folding frontispiece) of Mr.
Daniel Dancer and his sister, and also of Mr. Elwes, of Suffolk, and
transfers all the facts from those authentic narratives to Mr. Krook.
Twice when the dustman is called in to carry off a cartload of old
paper, ashes, and broken bottles, the whole court assembles and pries
into the baskets as they come forth. Many times the two gentlemen who
write with the ravenous little pens on the tissue-paper are seen
prowling in the neighbourhood—shy of each other, their late
partnership being dissolved. The Sol skilfully carries a vein of the
prevailing interest through the Harmonic nights. Little Swills, in
what are professionally known as “patter” allusions to the subject,
is received with loud applause; and the same vocalist “gags” in the
regular business like a man inspired. Even Miss M. Melvilleson, in
the revived Caledonian melody of “We’re a-Nodding,” points the
sentiment that “the dogs love broo” (whatever the nature of that
refreshment may be) with such archness and such a turn of the head
towards next door that she is immediately understood to mean Mr.
Smallweed loves to find money, and is nightly honoured with a double
encore. For all this, the court discovers nothing; and as Mrs. Piper
and Mrs. Perkins now communicate to the late lodger whose appearance
is the signal for a general rally, it is in one continual ferment to
discover everything, and more.
c39:p58.summary: The entire court becomes obsessed with Smallweed's search through Krook's possessions, inventing elaborate fantasies about hidden treasure. The narrator describes daily routines and even entertainment at the local pub incorporating references to the search.
c39:p58.best_quote: Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus' purse of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop.

c12:p67.text:
At length, one afternoon a little before sunset, when the bright
groups of figures which have for the last hour or two enlivened the
Ghost’s Walk are all dispersed and only Sir Leicester and my Lady
remain upon the terrace, Mr. Tulkinghorn appears. He comes towards
them at his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never
slackened. He wears his usual expressionless mask—if it be a
mask—and carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every
crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great
or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his
personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients;
he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.
c12:p67.summary: At sunset, Tulkinghorn finally appears, moving at his usual methodical pace with an expressionless mask, embodying mystery and unknown knowledge.
c12:p67.best_quote: He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.

c2:p12.text:
Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.
c2:p12.summary: Despite believing herself inscrutable, Lady Dedlock is perfectly understood and managed by tradespeople and servants who deliberately lead her and her circle by flattery and careful study of her preferences.
c2:p12.best_quote: who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput

c6:p68.text:
All this and a great deal more he told us, not only with the utmost
brilliancy and enjoyment, but with a certain vivacious
candour—speaking of himself as if he were not at all his own affair,
as if Skimpole were a third person, as if he knew that Skimpole had
his singularities but still had his claims too, which were the
general business of the community and must not be slighted. He was
quite enchanting. If I felt at all confused at that early time in
endeavouring to reconcile anything he said with anything I had
thought about the duties and accountabilities of life (which I am far
from sure of), I was confused by not exactly understanding why he was
free of them. That he WAS free of them, I scarcely doubted; he was so
very clear about it himself.
c6:p68.summary: Esther observes Skimpole's extraordinary candor and charm while noting her confusion about why society seems to excuse him from ordinary moral obligations.
c6:p68.best_quote: If I felt at all confused at that early time in endeavouring to reconcile anything he said with anything I had thought about the duties and accountabilities of life...I was confused by not exactly understanding why he was free of them

c8:p24.text:
“Bleak House; true. There is, in that city of London there, some
property of ours which is much at this day what Bleak House was then;
I say property of ours, meaning of the suit’s, but I ought to call it
the property of costs, for costs is the only power on earth that will
ever get anything out of it now or will ever know it for anything but
an eyesore and a heartsore. It is a street of perishing blind houses,
with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much
as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their
hinges and falling asunder, the iron rails peeling away in flakes of
rust, the chimneys sinking in, the stone steps to every door (and
every door might be death’s door) turning stagnant green, the very
crutches on which the ruins are propped decaying. Although Bleak
House was not in Chancery, its master was, and it was stamped with
the same seal. These are the Great Seal’s impressions, my dear, all
over England—the children know them!”
c8:p24.summary: Jarndyce describes a street of property nominally belonging to the Jarndyce suit but effectively owned by costs; the houses are in terrible decay, windowless, rusted, and desolate, bearing the Great Seal's mark of Chancery throughout England.
c8:p24.best_quote: It is a street of perishing blind houses, with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their hinges and falling asunder, the iron rails peeling away in flakes of rust, the chimneys sinking in, the stone steps to every door (and every door might be death's door) turning stagnant green

c62:p20.text:
“See,” he returned gaily, “what a sympathy there must be between us!
I have had nothing else, poor Rick excepted—it’s a large
exception—in my mind. When you came in, I was full of it. When shall
we give Bleak House its mistress, little woman?”
c62:p20.summary: John Jarndyce joyfully confirms that he has been preoccupied with thoughts of marriage to Esther and eagerly asks when they should set the wedding date.
c62:p20.best_quote: When you came in, I was full of it. When shall we give Bleak House its mistress, little woman?

c10:p9.text:
Like as he is to look at, so is his apartment in the dusk of the
present afternoon. Rusty, out of date, withdrawing from attention,
able to afford it. Heavy, broad-backed, old-fashioned,
mahogany-and-horsehair chairs, not easily lifted; obsolete tables
with spindle-legs and dusty baize covers; presentation prints of the
holders of great titles in the last generation or the last but one,
environ him. A thick and dingy Turkey-carpet muffles the floor where
he sits, attended by two candles in old-fashioned silver candlesticks
that give a very insufficient light to his large room. The titles on
the backs of his books have retired into the binding; everything that
can have a lock has got one; no key is visible. Very few loose papers
are about. He has some manuscript near him, but is not referring to
it. With the round top of an inkstand and two broken bits of
sealing-wax he is silently and slowly working out whatever train of
indecision is in his mind. Now the inkstand top is in the middle, now
the red bit of sealing-wax, now the black bit. That’s not it. Mr.
Tulkinghorn must gather them all up and begin again.
c10:p9.summary: Tulkinghorn's apartment is decorated with old-fashioned, heavy furniture, locked boxes, and dim candlelight; he sits working through some mental decision using sealing-wax and inkstand tops.
c10:p9.best_quote: everything that can have a lock has got one; no key is visible
